newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asian markets hit by Wall Street tumble.
newsitem.headline: Asian markets hit by Wall Street tumble.

text.p: Stock markets across Asia were battered on Friday after Wall Street's overnight tumble, with Tokyo's Nikkei average falling nearly two percent.

Tokyo's benchmark 225-share Nikkei average closed off 386.26 points, or 1.88 percent, at 20,166.90, after cracking under the weight of worries about the economy as well as the sharp fall in the United States, brokers said.
Sydney and Wellington also felt the weight of the New York fall, as did Hong Kong, but Taipei was flat as investors there looked more for factors from China than the United States.
Seoul ignored Wall Street and jumped more than two percent.
In New York, blue-chip stocks sank to their biggest loss since mid-July on Thursday as fresh signs of a surprisingly strong economy boosted long-term bond interest rates above seven percent.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended down 64.73 points at 5,647.65, its largest drop since July 15, when it closed with a loss of 161 points.
The fall hit hard in Tokyo, where investors are still jittery about a survey released on Wednesday which showed worse-than-expected confidence in the economy.
"The investment environment is bad," said Keiji Arai, a strategist at Sanyo Securities Co Ltd.
Analysts in Hong Kong said the Hang Seng index was also pulled down by the overnight fall in U.S. stocks and bonds, as well as by a large share placement by New World Development Co Ltd.
The Hang Seng lost 169.19 points, or 1.49 percent, to close at 11,159.02.

"I guess we have run up against a whole bunch of things today - with the long bond yield ticking up above seven percent and that large placement by New World," said Glenn Lesko, head of sales trading at HG Asia.
New Zealand lost more than 16 points in early trade, but recovered marginally to close down 10.77 points, or 0.48 percent, at 2,228.77.

"I suppose you could say that with the weaker Dow and selling in the bonds overnight, our market was always going to be down, but we've had a strong rally and it may have proved a good excuse to take profits," said Duncan Rutherford of ANZ Securities.
Sydney's All Ordinaries index also fell at the opening before pulling back to end down 10.6 points, or 0.47 percent, at 2,268.7. It dropped almost 15 points in the morning.
"It's off lows but that was mostly on the covering of positions in the afternoon," said Peter Struk, a dealer at Reynolds and Co.
The jump in Seoul was fueled by bargain hunting by domestic institutions and foreign investors which pushed the composite index up by 16.72 points to a provisional close of 782.88.

The Weighted Index in Taiwan was down 2.61 points, or just 0.04 percent, to 6,309.82 by midday as comments by Chinese President Jiang Zemin that political differences would not interfere with Taiwan-China economic ties overrode the Dow's fall.
Singapore's Straits Times Industrials index was down 12.29 points, or 0.57 percent, to 2,150.36 in late afternoon trade.
Bangkok was off 10.16 points to 1,095.43 and Kuala Lumpur was down 0.29 to 1,110.20 points, also both in late trade.
